transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-04
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: Enabled

[00:00] Avery Chen: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, i'm avery from redwood, and i'll run the intro. um quick roll call, marco from se is also here.
[00:10] Priya Nair: hi avery, priya here. thanks.
[00:12] Carlos Gomez: carlos joining.
[00:14] Ellen Park: ellen here.
[00:16] Samir Desai: samir on security.
[00:20] Avery Chen: awesome. goal for today is to map your top 3 workloads, agree on success criteria, and pick an integration runway — openai-compatible endpoints vs direct sdk, and how function calling and structured outputs will be validated.
[00:35] Priya Nair: sounds good, we want to make sure latency is reasonable, but also not blow the monthly model budget.
[00:40] Marco Silva: totally, when you say latency what buckets are you thinking? 95th percentile for interactive UI, or async?
[00:48] Priya Nair: the customer-facing chat needs sub-500ms 95pct for short prompts (under 200 tokens), search/retrieval rerank can be relaxed to 1.2s, and batch ingestion is background.
[00:58] Carlos Gomez: to add, our traffic is spiky — we have a big batch job every morning and then a peak window 12–2pm PT. we'll share histograms.
[01:10] Marco Silva: ok that matches common patterns. for spiky workloads we usually recommend a mix: dedicated for the sustained baseline and hosted burst capacity if you need headroom.
[01:22] Ellen Park: quick question on OpenAI compatibility — we have an existing integration using the openai SDK. migrating to a redwood endpoint, is it drop-in?
[01:29] Avery Chen: yes, we provide an openai-compatible endpoint layer; in many cases it's a header + endpoint swap. caveat: function calling/structured output can differ — we support the same function-calling semantics but there are nuances w/ streaming and partial completions.
[01:45] Priya Nair: what about embeddings? we currently use openai embeddings for semantic search.
[01:50] Marco Silva: embeddings are supported; you'll get the same vector shape. important to decide at POC whether you want our managed vector store or plug into your existing faiss/vespa cluster.
[02:03] Samir Desai: security wise we need SOC2 evidence, audit logs, KMS and SSO. also data residency constraints for EU PII — some customers must keep traces out of us-east.
[02:20] Avery Chen: we can provide SOC2 AICPA summary, audit log exports, and integrations with your KMS (supports AWS KMS and customer HSM). for residency we can pin model endpoints to regions. will pull security docs into the playbook.
[02:35] Priya Nair: great. can you also describe the benchmark plan — how you would validate quality regressions vs our current baseline?
[02:42] Marco Silva: short answer: we'll run a pairwise benchmark. you'll provide a set of representative prompts (ideally 200-500 prompts across intents), and we'll run them against your current baseline and the redwood-hosted model/variant. metrics: latency p50/p95, token cost, and quality metrics — BLEU-ish or human-rated pass/fail for structured outputs.
[03:05] Carlos Gomez: how do you capture structured output correctness? we rely on strict JSON with enums.
[03:10] Marco Silva: agreed. for structured output we use a schema validation step — validate JSON structure and field types, plus a small set of unit tests that assert business rules. we also capture hallucination rate by checking required fields and cross-field consistency.
[03:26] Ellen Park: if the model produces slightly malformed JSON in streaming, can your SDK repair or do we need post-processing?
[03:33] Marco Silva: we have a post-processor helper in the SDK that attempts deterministic repairs — but it's best to test with the same prompt set. streaming partial chunks are sometimes truncated; we recommend final-assembly and then schema validation.
[03:47] Priya Nair: on cost, can we do token-level breakdowns during the POC? like per-route cost for each intent?
[03:54] Avery Chen: yes, our console provides per-route token breakdown and you can instrument token counters in the SDK. for POC we'll give you a sample dashboard and the raw CSVs.
[04:03] Carlos Gomez: for the Dedicated option, how much lead time? we're thinking of reserved capacity if numbers justify it.
[04:09] Marco Silva: Dedicated provisioning typically takes 2–3 weeks for reserved pools, longer if it's a private on-prem package. but you can start with Hosted and convert to Dedicated with a planned migration window in the POC.
[04:22] Samir Desai: on encryption at rest — do you encrypt KV cache and model weights?
[04:26] Marco Silva: yes encryption at rest across disk, and customer-managed keys for encryption in Dedicated/Private plans. for hosted, we use provider KMS. KV cache encryption depends on deployment mode — we can enable it.
[04:38] Priya Nair: success criteria — let's put down three measurable items: 1) end-user latency under 500ms p95 for chat, 2) structured output acceptance > 98% on schema, 3) monthly cost within 1.3x of current baseline for same traffic.
[04:55] Avery Chen: sounds reasonable. i'll put those in the runbook. any other criteria?
[04:59] Ellen Park: reliability: we need 99.9% uptime during peak windows.
[05:03] Marco Silva: we'll map that to SLO targets and simulate failure modes in the POC if you want chaos testing.
[05:11] Priya Nair: timeline — we'd like results in 4 weeks. what's feasible?
[05:16] Marco Silva: 4 weeks is tight but doable: week 1: runbook + data collection, week 2: benchmark harness + smoke tests, week 3: full runs and tuning (quantization / batch configs), week 4: evaluation and handoff.
[05:29] Carlos Gomez: do you support quantized model variants for cost savings?
[05:32] Marco Silva: yes, we can run int8 or mixed-precision quantized variants; part of the tuning step is quality vs cost tradeoffs. we'll include recommended quantization profiles per intent.
[05:44] Priya Nair: about the SDKs — we use node for the backend and some python for offline jobs. do you have official SDKs?
[05:51] Avery Chen: official SDKs for node and python, plus a Golang community client. they support OpenAI-compatible request shapes, streaming, function calling helpers, and the structured output validators.
[06:05] Priya Nair: for function calling, can we register typed schemas and have the model prefer them?
[06:11] Marco Silva: yes, we support function definitions with parameter schemas. the runtime will surface function suggestions. in the POC we'll test required-field enforcement and edge cases.
[06:21] Ellen Park: our current worry is migration risk — what if behavior drifts? do you support canary rollouts?
[06:27] Marco Silva: yes, rollouts are first-class: canary routing, A/B tests, and automatic fallback to previous model variants based on quality metrics. we'll set thresholds for rollback.
[06:36] Priya Nair: regarding integrations with our infra — we have internal auth (OIDC) and request tracing. can your console ingest traces?
[06:43] Avery Chen: we have tracing hooks and you can send spans to our observability pipeline or integrate with your datadog/jaeger via exporters. auth: SSO/SAML + OIDC supported for the console.
[06:53] Carlos Gomez: can we run a short network latency test to your hosted region from our clusters?
[06:57] Avery Chen: yes, marco will share a tiny script. we usually do ping/tcp latency and a small handshake test to measure TLS roundtrip.
[07:06] Marco Silva: i'll add that to the repo, it's a couple lines and we'll include results format.
[07:13] Samir Desai: also need an ingestion data retention policy — during POC can you guarantee no training data retention?
[07:19] Marco Silva: for POC we can disable retention and ensure logs are ephemeral; long-term we can set retention windows per contract. we'll include a legal-safe statement in the runbook.
[07:30] Priya Nair: ok, let's talk benchmarks specifics — what harness do you propose?
[07:33] Marco Silva: we'll build a harness that can replay traffic at variable rates, with sampling for streaming vs non-streaming. metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens per request, cost estimate, success rate for schema, and a quality rubric (0–3) for selected prompts.
[07:50] Priya Nair: who does the human evals? we can do internal labeling but time may be limited.
[07:56] Avery Chen: we can help with initial human evals — a small redwood QA batch — but for product-specific labels we recommend Maven do the final pass.
[08:06] Ellen Park: can the harness simulate concurrency and KV cache effects? our workloads are chatty and benefit from persistent KV cache across sessions.
[08:15] Marco Silva: yes, the harness can simulate persistent sessions and warm KV caches. we'll test cold vs warm latency.
[08:26] Carlos Gomez: one more question on tooling: do you provide a structured-output diff tool to see where outputs deviate from expected schema across runs?
[08:33] Marco Silva: we do — an output comparison utility that highlights field-level diffs and aggregates failure reasons. we'll include sample reports in the POC deliverable.
[08:45] Priya Nair: great. i want all the artifacts: runbook, harness, raw results, and a short exec summary for the c-suite.
[08:52] Avery Chen: we'll produce a 1-page exec summary plus a longer technical appendix.
[08:56] Priya Nair: ok let's lock on the prompts — carlos will upload a representative set by friday.
[09:01] Carlos Gomez: yes, i'll share a csv and a small script to anonymize PII.
[09:06] Samir Desai: and i'll review the security playbook once you send it.
[09:09] Avery Chen: sounds good. i'll summarize next steps now.
[09:11] Avery Chen: recap: redwood to share POC runbook, security docs, benchmark harness + scripts, and network latency test; maven to share prompts, traffic histograms, and KMS requirements. aim to kick off next monday for week1.
[09:26] Ellen Park: ok thanks everyone.
[09:28] Priya Nair: thanks, bye.
[09:30] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: some technical terms may be slightly misrecognized (kay-v cache = KV cache, redwood dedicated sometimes transcribed as redwood dedicate).
